subChunks.title: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF — and When to Denormalise
subChunks.hookHtml: Normalisation is the process of organising a schema to eliminate redundancy and ensure each fact is stored exactly once. The normal forms are a progression from basic to rigorous.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
First Normal Form (1NF)

A table is in 1NF if:

  • Every column holds a single atomic value (no lists, no arrays in a cell)
  • No two rows are identical (there is a primary key)
-- VIOLATES 1NF: comma list in a cell
apprentice | spells
Alice      | 'Fireball, IceBlast, Shield'

-- CORRECT 1NF: separate rows
apprentice_id | spell
1             | Fireball
1             | IceBlast
1             | Shield

Second Normal Form (2NF)

Requires 1NF + no partial dependency (every non-key column must depend on the whole primary key, not just part of it). Only relevant for tables with composite PKs.

-- Composite PK: (apprentice_id, quest_id)
-- 'quest_title' depends only on quest_id (partial dependency) — violates 2NF
quest_completions(apprentice_id, quest_id, quest_title, score)

-- CORRECT: quest_title moves to quests table
quest_completions(apprentice_id, quest_id, score)
quests(id, title, ...)

Third Normal Form (3NF)

Requires 2NF + no transitive dependency (no non-key column depends on another non-key column).

-- mentor_specialty depends on mentor_id (not the primary key id)
apprentices(id, name, mentor_id, mentor_specialty)  -- violates 3NF

-- CORRECT: mentor_specialty moves to mentors table
mentors(id, name, specialty)
apprentices(id, name, mentor_id)  -- mentor_id FK → mentors

When to denormalise

Normalised schemas are query-friendly for writes. Sometimes you deliberately denormalise for read performance: precomputing totals, flattening joins for reporting tables, using JSON columns for flexible attributes.

storyBeats.text: The schema has a column for mentor name AND mentor specialty in the apprentices table. When a mentor changes specialty, two tables must be updated.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: 1NF: one value per cell. 2NF: every column depends on the whole key. 3NF: no column depends on another non-key column. Follow these rules and each fact lives in exactly one place. Break them deliberately only when the query performance gains outweigh the update complexity.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Normalisation exercise

Identify which normal form each violation breaks and write the corrected schema:

-- Table: order_items
-- PK: (order_id, product_id)
order_items(
  order_id, product_id,
  product_name,   -- (1)
  customer_email, -- (2)
  quantity
)
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
(1) product_name — violates 2NF. product_name depends only on product_id (part of the composite PK), not on the whole (order_id, product_id). Fix: move product_name to a products(id, name, ...) table.

(2) customer_email — violates 3NF (and 2NF). It depends on order_id only, which is part of the composite PK — but only part of it (2NF violation). More specifically it depends on a non-key fact about the order. Fix: move customer_email to an orders(id, customer_email, ...) table.

Corrected schema:
products(id PK, name, price)
customers(id PK, email, name)
orders(id PK, customer_id FK, placed_at)
order_items(order_id FK, product_id FK, quantity, PRIMARY KEY(order_id, product_id))
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Describe a real-world scenario where you would deliberately denormalise a 3NF schema for performance reasons. What is the trade-off?
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Scenario: a reporting dashboard that displays total orders, revenue, and average order value per customer for the past 30 days. The normalised query joins orders → order_items → products and aggregates across millions of rows — it takes 8 seconds.

Denormalisation: add a customer_stats table (customer_id, total_orders, total_revenue, avg_order_value) refreshed nightly by a batch job. The dashboard reads from customer_stats in milliseconds.

Trade-off: the data is up to 24 hours stale. If an order is placed in the morning, it will not appear in the dashboard until the next refresh. Write complexity increases — the batch job or triggers must keep customer_stats consistent. Choose denormalisation when staleness is acceptable and the read-performance gain is worth the write complexity.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF in plain English with one example of a violation for each. Why does 2NF only matter for composite primary keys?

options: Each column holds a single atomic value and there are no duplicate rows
Every non-key column depends on the whole primary key
No non-key column depends on another non-key column
All columns have the same data type
questions.answer: Each column holds a single atomic value and there are no duplicate rows
questions.explanation: First Normal Form requires atomicity (one value per cell) and a primary key (no duplicate rows). Storing comma-delimited lists in a column violates 1NF.

questions.prompt: A table has composite PK (user_id, course_id) and a column `course_title`. What normal form does this violate?
options: 2NF — course_title depends only on course_id, not on the full composite key
No violation — composite PKs allow partial dependencies
questions.answer: 2NF — course_title depends only on course_id, not on the full composite key
questions.explanation: Second Normal Form requires that all non-key columns depend on the entire primary key. course_title depends only on course_id (part of the PK) — this is a partial dependency, violating 2NF. Fix: move course_title to a courses table.

questions.prompt: In `employees(id, dept_id, dept_name)`, what normal form does dept_name violate?
options: 3NF — dept_name depends on dept_id (a non-key column), not on id (the primary key)
2NF — dept_name does not depend on the full PK
No violation — the column depends on a key
questions.answer: 3NF — dept_name depends on dept_id (a non-key column), not on id (the primary key)
questions.explanation: Third Normal Form requires no transitive dependencies: non-key → non-key. dept_name depends on dept_id, and dept_id depends on id. The chain id → dept_id → dept_name is a transitive dependency. Fix: move dept_name to a departments table.

questions.prompt: You have a fully normalised schema for an e-commerce site. The home page product listing query joins 6 tables and takes 2 seconds. What is the best approach?
options: Denormalise strategically — create a product_listing_view or product_search table with the flattened data, refreshed periodically
Normalise further — the slow query suggests the schema is not normalised enough
Replace SQL with a NoSQL database
questions.answer: Denormalise strategically — create a product_listing_view or product_search table with the flattened data, refreshed periodically
questions.explanation: More normalisation does not improve query performance — it typically adds more joins. Denormalisation for read-heavy, latency-sensitive paths is a deliberate performance optimisation. A cached/materialised read model (product_listing_view) is the standard solution.
